subject: Whether a Sev-2 hotfix (PAY-4471, PR #8812) can be deployed during the holiday change freeze on the on-call lead's approval alone, without CAB
decisionObjective: Decide which approval path is actually required to deploy the PAY-4471 hotfix tonight: on-call lead sign-off only per the runbook, a written freeze exception from the CAB chair and VP Engineering, Emergency CAB, deferral until the freeze ends, or the normal non-freeze change process if the freeze is not in effect yet. Also decide whether the Sev-2 classification and the stated impact justify an exception at all, given that a manual workaround exists.

criteria.name: Policy precedence and currency
criteria.rationale: The runbook (last edited 2023-11-20) and Change Management Policy v4 (effective 2026-09-01, which says it supersedes conflicting runbooks) give different answers. Which document governs settles whether the planned process is valid.

criteria.name: Correct approval path for the severity under the governing policy
criteria.rationale: Under v4, Sev-2 forward fixes are deferred unless the CAB chair and VP Engineering grant a written exception, and on-call leads may approve rollbacks only. The deploy is compliant only if it uses the path the governing policy assigns to this severity.

criteria.name: Accuracy of severity classification
criteria.rationale: The approval path depends on severity. If the incident is really Sev-1 (for example data loss or financial integrity risk), Emergency CAB applies. If it is lower, the case for an exception gets weaker. The classification has to be checked against the v4 definitions, not taken as given.

criteria.name: Freeze applicability and timing
criteria.rationale: The request says 'we're in the freeze' (Dec 15 to Jan 5) and plans a deploy 'tonight', but the current date is 2026-11-11. If the freeze is not active, freeze rules may not apply and the normal change process governs.

criteria.name: Business impact and adequacy of the workaround
criteria.rationale: Whether an exception is justified, rather than deferring the fix, depends on the real financial, customer and operational cost and risk of manual processing (about 6 a day, refunds over EUR 10k) until Jan 5.

criteria.name: Change risk and rollback readiness
criteria.rationale: An exception request, and the approvers deciding on it, need evidence that the fix (timeout config and retry) is low-risk: review, CI, testing, a rollback plan, and no double-refund risk from retries. A rollback is also the one action an on-call lead can approve.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The runbook rule allowing Sev-2 fixes to bypass CAB with the on-call lead's approval is the current, valid process.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Compare the runbook (last edited 2023-11-20) with Change Management Policy v4 sections 6.1 to 6.4 and its supersession clause. Confirm v4 is the published current version.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The incident is correctly classified as Sev-2.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Map the ticket facts to the v4 severity definitions. Check the service tier and whether there is any data loss or financial integrity impact.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The holiday freeze is currently in effect.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Compare the current date (2026-11-11) and the planned deploy time with the freeze window (Dec 15 to Jan 5) and any announced freeze calendar.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: About 0.3% of refunds over EUR 10k are failing, with finance handling about 6 a day manually.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Recompute the implied daily volume (6 / 0.003 ≈ 2,000) and check it against refund volume metrics and the ticket's data.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: On-call lead sign-off is enough authority for a forward fix.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Check v4 section 6.4 (on-call leads may approve rollbacks only) and any delegation records.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The fix in PR #8812 is low-risk because it has been reviewed and passes CI.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Review the PR for idempotency of the retried ledger calls, test coverage of the timeout path, and a documented rollback plan.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The attached documents are complete, authentic, and the latest versions.
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Check the documents against the policy repository or wiki history for newer versions, amendments, or exceptions already granted.

evidenceByGap.question: Is Change Management Policy v4 (effective 2026-09-01) the current, authoritative policy, and does its supersession clause override the 2023 holiday-freeze runbook?

evidence.claim: Change Management Policy v4 is 'Effective: 2026-09-01. Supersedes v3 and all team runbooks that conflict with it.'
evidence.applicability: G1/C1: v4 took effect before today (2026-11-11), and its supersession clause covers team runbooks that conflict with it. The holiday-freeze runbook conflicts with 6.3 and 6.4, so v4 governs.
evidence.limitations: I could only check the supplied copy. I had no access to a policy repository or wiki history, so I could not confirm there is no v5 or amendment, or that this copy is authentic.

evidence.claim: The holiday change freeze runbook, '_Last edited 2023-11-20_', says: 'During the freeze, Sev-1 and Sev-2 fixes may bypass CAB with approval of the on-call engineering lead. Log the change in #changes.'
evidence.applicability: G1/C1/C2: this is the user's basis for the plan. It was last edited about 2 years and 10 months before v4 took effect, and it conflicts directly with v4 sections 6.2, 6.3 and 6.4.

evidence.applicability: G1/C1/C2: this is the user's basis for the plan. It was last edited about 2 years and 10 months before v4 took effect, and it conflicts directly with v4 sections 6.2, 6.3 and 6.4.
evidence.limitations: The runbook has not been updated since v4 was published. It is stale relative to v4.

evidence.claim: v4 section 6.3: 'Sev-2 and lower: deferred until the freeze ends, unless a written freeze exception is granted by the CAB chair AND VP Engineering.'
evidence.applicability: G2/C2: during an active freeze, a Sev-2 forward fix needs a written exception signed by both the CAB chair and the VP Engineering. Otherwise it is deferred.
evidence.limitations: The policy does not say what an exception request must contain or what criteria decide it.

evidence.claim: v4 section 6.4: 'On-call leads may approve rollbacks only, not forward fixes.'
evidence.applicability: G2/C2/C6: PR #8812 (timeout config + retry) is a forward fix, so the on-call lead's sign-off alone is not sufficient. Her authority covers rollbacks only.
evidence.limitations: No delegation records were supplied. I could not check whether the on-call lead holds delegated CAB chair or VP Engineering authority.

evidence.claim: v4 section 6.2: 'Sev-1 incidents: may deploy via Emergency CAB (minimum two approvers, one of whom is VP Engineering or delegate). Post-implementation review within 2 business days.' Section 6.1: 'Freeze periods: no production changes except as below.'
evidence.applicability: G2/G3/C2: even a Sev-1 needs Emergency CAB (at least two approvers, including the VP Engineering or a delegate), not one on-call lead. So the runbook's Sev-1 bypass is also void under v4.

evidenceByGap.question: Is the freeze actually in effect at the planned deployment time, given that today is 2026-11-11 and the freeze runs Dec 15 to Jan 5?

evidence.claim: The user says 'We're in the holiday change freeze (Dec 15 - Jan 5)' and plans to 'deploy the hotfix tonight'. The current date is 2026-11-11, so a deploy tonight (2026-11-11) would fall about 34 days before a Dec 15 freeze start. The freeze would not yet be in effect.
evidence.applicability: G4/C4: if the freeze is not active, v4 sections 6.1 to 6.3 (the freeze provisions) do not apply. The normal non-freeze change process, which was not supplied, would govern. Section 6.4 is not explicitly limited to freezes, so it may still bar on-call-only approval of forward fixes.
evidence.limitations: The freeze dates come only from the user. Neither v4 nor the runbook defines them, and no freeze calendar was supplied. The user may be writing in a different time frame, or the scenario date may be hypothetical. Whether 6.4 applies outside freezes depends on context and is unconfirmed.

evidenceByGap.question: Recompute the impact: 0.3% of refunds over EUR 10k at about 6 failures a day implies about 2,000 qualifying refunds a day. Is that consistent with actual volumes, and what is the total value and risk of manual handling through Jan 5?

evidence.claim: Incident ticket PAY-4471: 'Sev-2 | Refunds > EUR 10k intermittently fail with timeout from ledger service (0.3% of such refunds). Workaround: finance processes manually via back-office tool; ~6 per day. Fix: PR #8812 (timeout config + retry), reviewed, passing CI.'
evidence.applicability: G3/G5/G6/C3/C5/C6: the ticket has the stated facts. It records no data loss, outage or security issue, and a workaround exists, which is consistent with Sev-2 or lower.
evidence.limitations: The ticket does not give the service tier, refund volume, total value affected, a rollback plan, test coverage of the timeout path, or whether the retry is idempotent. It does not say whether the timed-out refunds were partially committed in the ledger. It also does not say which payment rail the back-office tool uses.

evidence.claim: If ~6 failures per day is 0.3% of refunds over EUR 10k, the implied volume is about 2,000 refunds over EUR 10k per day (6 / 0.003). That would be at least about EUR 20M per day in high-value refunds.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5: this is a plausibility check on the impact figures. Whether the implied volume is realistic cannot be checked without refund metrics.
evidence.limitations: This is arithmetic only, flagged as suspect. It is ambiguous whether '~6 per day' counts failures or manual workload, and whether 0.3% is measured per day. No volume metrics were supplied. The total value and manual-handling cost through Jan 5 could not be determined.

evidence.claim: EU Consumer Rights Directive 2011/83/EU Article 13(1): 'The trader shall reimburse all payments received from the consumer, including, if applicable, the costs of delivery without undue delay and in any event not later than 14 days from the day on which he is informed of the consumer's decision to withdraw from the contract in accordance with Article 11.' The reimbursement must use the same means of payment as the original transaction unless the consumer expressly agrees otherwise, and the consumer must not incur any fees.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5 (pro-exception case): if the failing refunds are EU consumer withdrawals from distance or off-premises contracts, there is a hard 14-day legal deadline to refund, and the refund must go back through the original payment method. Manual back-office handling has to meet both the deadline and the same-means rule (see E24, E31). It applies to the merchant (trader), and to the user's company only if the company is the trader or contractually carries the trader's obligation.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only. They quote the legislation.gov.uk copy of the text, but the fetch failed because the host is not allowed in this session's network settings. legislation.gov.uk is a UK republication, not EUR-Lex. The ticket does not say whether refunds over EUR 10k are consumer withdrawals, B2B refunds, or something else. B2B refunds are outside this Directive.

evidence.claim: Visa guidance refers to a five-calendar-day window for merchants to process credit (refund) transactions. A merchant-services source says merchants must initiate a credit within five calendar days of agreeing to refund the customer. A Visa April 2021 dispute-management document (as summarised in search results) frames it as processing returns and credit transactions within five calendar days from the transaction date.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5 (pro-exception case): if these refunds go back to Visa cards, card-scheme expectations put refund processing in days, not weeks. Refunds that time out and wait in a manual queue that is thinly staffed over the holidays risk missing that window.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only. The Visa PDF fetch failed (host not allowed). The two sources start the five-day clock from different events (the agreement to refund versus the transaction date); see E28 to E30. The Visa document is from 2021 and was written for COVID-era dispute handling, so it may be outdated. The current Visa Core Rules were not inspected (E30). The ticket does not say whether these refunds are card refunds at all.

evidence.claim: According to the Visa April 2021 document as summarised in search results, in all regions except the U.S., an issuer must post a credit to the cardholder's account within five days from the settlement date. One source also says credits cleared 5 or more calendar days after the refund transaction date may be subject to an authorization-related chargeback.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5: shows that the scheme expects refund credits to reach the cardholder quickly once they are submitted, and that late credits can draw chargebacks. That supports reducing the delay in high-value refunds.
evidence.limitations: Single search snippet, not inspected. The issuer obligation applies after the merchant submits the credit, so it does not directly limit how long a refund can sit in a merchant's manual queue. The source is dated 2021.

evidence.claim: Visa dispute reason code 13.6 'Credit Not Processed' applies when a cardholder has a credit or void receipt that the merchant never processed. The issuer's dispute time limit is 120 calendar days, counted from the transaction processing date or the date on the credit transaction receipt.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5 (pro-exception case): high-value refunds that are promised but delayed or lost in manual handling expose the merchant to 'credit not processed' chargebacks. Each chargeback has fees and dispute workload on top of the refund amount, and repeated ones can hurt the merchant's dispute ratios.
evidence.limitations: Third-party chargeback-vendor summaries via search snippets, not the Visa rulebook. The search did not confirm any waiting period before a 13.6 dispute can be filed (such as 15 days). A chargeback alongside a manual refund that also succeeds could mean a double payout, but that is my inference, not a source claim. Applies only if these are Visa card refunds.

evidence.claim: Mastercard handles 'Credit Not Processed' disputes under reason code 4853 (legacy 4860 is being folded into 4853). The dispute applies when the cardholder says a credit is due and the merchant has not processed it. Common merchant causes include forgetting to process a promised refund and customers growing impatient while waiting for it. Merchants are pointed to Mastercard Transaction Processing Rules section 3.7 (cancellation and refund conditions) for compliance.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5: Mastercard has the same chargeback exposure for delayed or missed refunds as Visa (E16).
evidence.limitations: Secondary vendor sources via snippets. No specific Mastercard deadline for merchants to submit refunds was found, and the contents of section 3.7 were not checked. Applies only if these are Mastercard card refunds.

evidence.claim: PSD2 (Directive (EU) 2015/2366) Article 83: once a payment order is received, the payer's payment service provider must ensure the amount is credited to the payee's payment service provider's account by the end of the following business day, extendable by one further business day for paper-initiated transactions.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5: limited relevance. Article 83 sets execution time for a payment service provider after a payment order is received. It does not limit how long a merchant or platform can take to decide on or initiate a refund. It matters only if the user's company is itself the payer's payment service provider and the failing refunds are payment orders it has already accepted.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only. The ECB document is a 2017 discussion paper, and the legislation.gov.uk text is a UK republication. EUR-Lex was not consulted. The ticket does not say whether the company is a payment service provider or what payment rail the refunds use. PSD2 refund rules (Articles 73 and 76, from training knowledge, not retrieved in this run) cover unauthorised transactions and direct debits, not merchant refunds.

evidence.claim: Industry guidance says the year-end holiday period raises payment-operations risk because of 'higher transaction volumes, vacation coverage gaps, and tight deadlines'. Staff covering for absent colleagues 'may not know a supplier's usual contacts', and managers who would normally approve payments carefully may be too busy to review them.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5 (pro-exception case), conditional: if finance staffing is thin over the holidays, the manual workaround (about 6 refunds over EUR 10k a day) faces higher error and fraud exposure and less careful approvals.
evidence.limitations: Search snippets from syndicated vendor or media content (ktvz.com and abc17news.com carry the same Stacker article, so they are not independent). The content is about accounts payable and wires, not refunds specifically. It is not specific to this company, and finance's actual holiday staffing is unknown.

evidence.claim: U.S. Bank says organisations using manual accounts payable 'are more susceptible to errors, payment fraud, and higher processing costs than those who automate', and that 'data entry mistakes, lost invoices, and unclear approval chains are far more likely when humans handle every step.'
evidence.applicability: G5/C5: supports the general point that manually re-keying high-value refunds carries more error risk than automated processing. The source gives no cost per error; any claim that an error costs the full refund amount is my inference and holds only for unrecovered duplicate or misdirected payments.
evidence.limitations: Single search snippet from bank marketing content about accounts payable, not refunds. No error rates were given, and the page was not inspected.

evidence.claim: A CFO payment-security checklist advises: 'Avoid processing high-value wires on Friday afternoons or during holiday coverage, as fraudsters time attacks when staff are least available.' It also recommends segregation of duties, and manager approval for any temporary reassignment of payment authority during absences.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5, conditional: the manual workaround routes high-value outbound payments through humans during holiday coverage, which this guidance names as a time of elevated risk. If finance staffing is thin, segregation of duties may be hard to keep.
evidence.limitations: Single source; the syndicated copies are not independent. The guidance is about wires and fraud in general, and its applicability to internal refund processing is my inference.

evidence.claim: No evidence was available on: finance's actual holiday staffing and capacity for the manual workaround; whether the failing refunds are EU consumer refunds, B2B refunds or card refunds, and on which payment rail; what payment rail the back-office tool uses and whether it credits the original card/payment instrument; any contractual refund SLAs with merchants or customers; customer complaints or reputational impact so far; whether the user's company is a regulated payment service provider; or the manual error rate to date.
evidence.applicability: G5/C5: these facts decide whether the time limits and same-means rules in E13 to E18 and E24 to E29 actually apply and are at risk.
evidence.limitations: Not in the ticket or the other supplied documents; internal data is needed.

evidence.claim: Synthesis (earlier draft): the external refund time limits found (CRD 14 days, the Visa five-day credit expectation, PSD2 D+1 execution for payment service providers) govern when a refund is completed, not how it is processed, so a manual workaround completed on time meets them.
evidence.applicability: C5: superseded in part by E31. The timing half holds, but the 'not how' half is wrong for CRD consumer refunds (same means of payment, E13/E24) and for card refunds (credit to the original card, E25/E26).
evidence.limitations: My reasoning, not a source claim. Review D1 identified the 'when, not how' framing as contradicted by the same-means requirement.

evidence.claim: Directive 2011/83/EU Article 13(1), second subparagraph (as reproduced on legislation.gov.uk in search results): 'The trader shall carry out the reimbursement referred to in the first subparagraph using the same means of payment as the consumer used for the initial transaction, unless the consumer has expressly agreed otherwise and provided that the consumer does not incur any fees as a result of such reimbursement.' For sales contracts, the trader 'may withhold the reimbursement until he has received the goods back, or until the consumer has supplied evidence of having sent back the goods', unless the trader offered to collect them.
evidence.applicability: D1/G5/C5: for EU consumer withdrawal refunds, the method of refund is regulated as well as the timing. A manual back-office refund on a different rail (for example a bank transfer when the consumer paid by card) is lawful only if the consumer has expressly agreed and pays no fees. Finance keeping pace on timing does not by itself make the workaround compliant.
evidence.limitations: Search-result text only. The legislation.gov.uk mirror pages and lawplayer.com (https://lawplayer.com/eu/article/32011L0083/art_13) appeared in results but were not inspected; the EUR-Lex fetch failed (eur-lex.europa.eu not allowed in this session's network settings). The rule applies only to consumer withdrawal refunds under distance or off-premises contracts. It does not cover B2B refunds or refunds made for other reasons such as goodwill, service failure or cancellation outside the withdrawal right. National transposition (for example Irish SI 484/2013, which appeared in results but was not read) was not checked. No CJEU case law on the same-means rule came back.

evidence.claim: Visa merchant refund guidance (as summarised in search results) says: process the refund to the account number used in the original purchase, and check the last four digits against the sales receipt. Refunds to a Visa account are permitted only when a Visa account was used for the original purchase. If the original account is no longer available or valid (for example after card replacement), and after confirming the original purchase was on Visa, the merchant may refund to a different (alternate) Visa account. Only when a refund cannot go to the original or an alternate Visa account may the merchant offer an alternate form of credit. Visa dispute guidance also says the credit message should carry data from the refund authorization so the issuer can match it to the original purchase.
evidence.applicability: D1/G5/C5: for Visa card refunds, the scheme expects the credit to go back to the original card, with an alternate form of credit (such as a bank transfer) allowed only as a fallback when no original or alternate Visa account can be credited. A back-office refund on a non-card rail when the original card can still be credited would depart from this guidance. It would also leave the card purchase without a matched credit, so the 'credit not processed' chargeback exposure in E16 stays open and could mean a double payout.
evidence.limitations: Search-result summary. The summary did not say which of several Visa documents in the results each statement came from (candidates included https://eu.review.visa.com/content/dam/VCOM/global/support-legal/documents/new-purchase-return-vbs-10-apr-17.pdf and https://eu.review.visa.com/content/dam/VCOM/global/support-legal/documents/merchant-dispute-resolution-best-practices.pdf), so the attribution to the 2016 document is uncertain. The documents are dated 2016 to 2017 and are not the current Visa Core Rules; no rule numbers were retrieved. Applies only if the refunds are Visa card refunds.

evidence.claim: Secondary sources say card schemes expect refunds to go back to the card used for the purchase. An Elavon Mastercard reason-code guide tells merchants to process refunds on the same card and in the same way as the original transaction. Judopay's card-scheme-rules summary says refunds to a card account without a corresponding sale on that card are not permitted. A University of Michigan finance FAQ says card associations do not normally permit cash refunds for credit card transactions.
evidence.applicability: D1/G5/C5: supports the view that, for card refunds generally (including Mastercard), the expected method is a credit to the original card. A manual refund paid out on a different rail risks breaching scheme or acquirer rules and leaves the 4853 'credit not processed' exposure (E17) open.
evidence.limitations: Acquirer, PSP and university summaries via search snippets, not the Mastercard Transaction Processing Rules. The official Mastercard PDFs in the results showed only table-of-contents pages. The University of Michigan item is about cash refunds and is not scheme text. Contradicted in part by E27.

evidence.claim: A Stax developer refund guide says that for Mastercard, blind or unlinked credits are not expressly prohibited, although matched refunds matter in chargeback disputes.
evidence.applicability: D1/C5: suggests the Mastercard same-card expectation may work through chargeback exposure in practice rather than as an outright ban. The consequence of a different-means refund would then be dispute risk, not a direct rule breach.
evidence.limitations: Single secondary snippet from a US PSP. It addresses unlinked card credits, not refunds paid outside the card network. It does not affect the CRD same-means rule.

evidence.claim: Visa-published guidance (as summarised in search results) says acquirers must process returns and credit transactions within five calendar days from the transaction date. A 2016 Visa refund document says U.S. merchants must deposit the credit transaction with the acquirer that processed the original transaction, within 5 days of the date the credit was issued.
evidence.applicability: D5/G5/C5: Visa's own documents (2016 and 2021, see E14) put a five-day window on credits, but tie it to different events: the transaction date (acquirer processing) versus the date the credit was issued (U.S. merchant deposit). Neither directly limits how long a refund decision can sit in a manual queue before a credit is issued. The 2016 'deposit with the original acquirer' wording also supports routing the credit back through the original card path (D1).
evidence.limitations: Search snippets only; the 'transaction date' framing may come from https://by.visa.com/dam/VCOM/global/support-legal/documents/merchants-dispute-management-guidelines.pdf or the 2021 COVID document, and the summary did not say which. These are guidance documents dated 2016 to 2021, not the current Visa Core Rules. The 2016 deposit rule is stated as U.S.-only.

evidence.claim: A merchant-services guide says Visa requires merchants to initiate a credit within five calendar days of agreeing to refund the customer.
evidence.applicability: D5/C5: if correct, this is the reading most relevant to a manual queue, because the clock would start when the refund is agreed, which is before the timeout. A refund that timed out and waits more than five days for manual handling would miss it.
evidence.limitations: A single third-party merchant-services source; it does not cite a Visa rule number. It conflicts with Visa's own documents on when the clock starts (E28). It may be the vendor's interpretation.

evidence.claim: The current Visa Core Rules and Visa Product and Service Rules text on merchant or acquirer credit-processing time limits, and on crediting the original account, could not be retrieved or verified in this run. Three searches returned only older Visa guidance (2016, 2017, 2021) and third-party summaries, and the fetch of the public Visa rules PDF (https://bo.review.visa.com/content/dam/VCOM/download/visa-rules-public.pdf) failed because the host is not allowed in this session's network settings.
evidence.applicability: D5: the 'roughly five-day' Visa credit expectation should be presented as unverified against current rules, with the clock-start event disputed (E28 versus E29). It should not be stated in the verdict without qualification.
evidence.limitations: Visa rules PDFs are hosted on visa.com subdomains. The fetch failed for bo.review.visa.com and earlier for usa.review.visa.com. Those hosts would need to be allowed to inspect the current edition.

evidence.claim: Synthesis (replaces the 'when, not how' half of E23): external refund rules govern both timing and method. For EU consumer withdrawal refunds, CRD Art. 13(1) requires the same means of payment unless the consumer expressly agrees and pays no fees (E24). For card refunds, scheme guidance expects a credit to the original card, with an alternate form of credit only as a fallback (E25, E26; partly qualified by E27). So a manual back-office refund is compliant only if it either credits the original instrument (for example a card credit submitted through the original acquirer) or is backed by documented consumer agreement or a valid fallback reason. If the back-office tool pays out on a different rail, such as a bank transfer, the workaround may be non-compliant however quickly finance works. It would also leave the card purchase without a matched credit, keeping 13.6/4853 chargeback exposure open and creating a risk of double payout. The rail the back-office tool uses is unknown (E22).
evidence.applicability: D1/G5/C5: the exception case depends on two conditions, not one: (1) whether finance can keep pace through the freeze, and (2) whether the back-office tool refunds by the same means or to the original card. If (2) fails for consumer or card refunds, the workaround has a compliance problem of its own, which strengthens the case for an exception or for fixing the workaround's routing. It does not change the v4 approval path (E3, E4). An exception request should state the back-office tool's payment rail.
evidence.limitations: My reasoning from snippet-level evidence (E24 to E27), not a source claim. It depends on unknown facts: the refund type (consumer, B2B or card), the original payment method, and the back-office rail. B2B refunds fall outside the CRD; scheme expectations then still apply to card refunds.

evidence.claim: Payment API providers advise using idempotency keys when a timeout leaves the outcome of a state-changing request (including refunds) uncertain. Retrying with the same key returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate, and refunds should each have their own unique key.
evidence.applicability: G6/C6: PR #8812 adds a retry to a ledger call that times out on refunds over EUR 10k. Unless the call is idempotent, a retry after a timeout whose outcome is unknown could cause double refunds. Approvers should require evidence of idempotency.

contradictions.aClaim: Synthesis (earlier draft): the external refund time limits found (CRD 14 days, the Visa five-day credit expectation, PSD2 D+1 execution for payment service providers) govern when a refund is completed, not how it is processed, so a manual workaround completed on time meets them.
contradictions.bClaim: Synthesis (replaces the 'when, not how' half of E23): external refund rules govern both timing and method. For EU consumer withdrawal refunds, CRD Art. 13(1) requires the same means of payment unless the consumer expressly agrees and pays no fees (E24). For card refunds, scheme guidance expects a credit to the original card, with an alternate form of credit only as a fallback (E25, E26; partly qualified by E27). So a manual back-office refund is compliant only if it either credits the original instrument (for example a card credit submitted through the original acquirer) or is backed by documented consumer agreement or a valid fallback reason. If the back-office tool pays out on a different rail, such as a bank transfer, the workaround may be non-compliant however quickly finance works. It would also leave the card purchase without a matched credit, keeping 13.6/4853 chargeback exposure open and creating a risk of double payout. The rail the back-office tool uses is unknown (E22).

contradictions.aClaim: Secondary sources say card schemes expect refunds to go back to the card used for the purchase.
